final_answer:
SHORT ANSWER. Yes, but the I-130/I-485 denials cannot be fixed first or in isolation. The husband's practical path is (1) a motion to reopen and rescind the August 1, 2025 in absentia order before the immigration judge (IJ), based on lack of proper notice, and (2) separately repairing the I-130 with USCIS. The I-485 can only be re-adjudicated afterwards, by the IJ in reopened proceedings, once a valid I-130 is approved or pending.

1. IMMIGRATION COURT: WHAT TO FILE. File a motion to reopen to rescind the in absentia order under INA 240(b)(5)(C)(ii), 8 U.S.C. 1229a(b)(5)(C)(ii), and 8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii), with the immigration court that entered the order. A lack-of-notice motion may be filed at any time, so the 180-day limit (exceptional circumstances, 240(b)(5)(C)(i)) does not bar it, and the order is nearly 8 months old as of April 1, 2026 (the 180 days ran about January 28, 2026, so the exceptional-circumstances ground is likely untimely and should not be the lead argument). Only one such motion is allowed per order. Filing the motion automatically stays removal until the IJ rules (8 CFR 1003.23(b)(4)(ii); INA 240(b)(5)(C)). The stay is a filing-based protection, so file promptly; ICE enforcement against an order that is a few months old is a real risk. The motion should be filed in the IJ's e-filing system (ECAS) or on paper with the court, with a cover page, a proposed order, proof of service on DHS/ICE OPLA, a Form EOIR-33 change of address (and EOIR-28 if represented), and sworn declarations from the husband and wife. The declarations should establish that: the only address ever given to DHS was the one on the I-130/I-485 forms, which the NTA did not use; no one lived at or received mail at the NTA address; no NTA, hearing notice or RFE was received; the couple continued to believe the cases were pending; and the husband learned of the order only on April 1, 2026. Attach the I-130/I-485 receipts and filings showing the correct address, the USCIS RFE/denial envelopes or notices showing the wrong address, and the EOIR automated case information printout. Ask the IJ to rescind the order, reopen and terminate or reset the case.

MERITS OF NOTICE. Under INA 239(a)(1) the NTA must be sent to the alien (or counsel) and 239(c) permits service by mail only to the last address the alien provided. Where the government mailed the NTA to an address the alien never provided, the alien has a strong argument that he did not receive notice under 239(a)(1) or (2); there is no 239(a)(2) change-of-time/place notice that cures it if that notice also went to the wrong address. Caution: Campos-Chaves v. Garland (2024) holds the alien must show lack of notice under both (a)(1) and (a)(2) for the hearing missed, so every notice (NTA and hearing notice) must be traced to the wrong address; and Niz-Chavez v. Garland requires a single complete NTA for stop-time purposes (not for this motion's outcome). Also expect DHS to argue that the husband had a duty to keep an address on file with the court (INA 239(a)(1)(F); EOIR-33) and that, because the NTA and hearing notices are mailed to the address of record, the presumption of delivery applies. If the court mailed notice to the address of record and the husband never gave the court an address, that issue must be investigated (obtain the ROP/ECAS record) because it may defeat the argument. Also note: the NTA was reportedly sent by USCIS. Whether USCIS issued the NTA after denying the I-485 (which is standard) and when it was filed with the court should be confirmed from the record.

2. FEES. Based on secondary sources (I could not open EOIR primary fee pages because of network blocks), a motion to reopen an in absentia order under 240(b)(5)(C)(ii) for lack of notice is exempt from the EOIR motion-to-reopen fee that otherwise applies (about $920 in FY2026 after OBBBA/H.R.1 inflation adjustment), so no fee should be due. By contrast, the exceptional-circumstances motion (240(b)(5)(C)(i)) carries the fee. One secondary summary of the interim PM 25-36 stated a $145 regulatory fee plus a $900 H.R.1 fee for the (ii) motion, which conflicts with other sources; PM 25-36 was reported rescinded by PM 26-01 (effective Jan. 2, 2026) as to the asylum fee, so the status is not fully resolved. Confirm on EOIR's fee page before filing; if the court rejects it for non-payment, a fee waiver (EOIR-26A) is where a waiver is permitted. If reopened and the husband wants the IJ to decide an I-485 (a new application), a separate EOIR adjustment fee (reported at roughly $1,600 for EOIR-42B-type applications) and the USCIS-type I-485 requirements would apply later; this figure is unverified. No fee is charged to file the proof of service or change of address.

3. THE I-130 DENIAL (USCIS). The RFE went to an address never provided, so the denial for failure to respond (abandonment/ 8 CFR 103.2(b)(13), (b)(8)) is vulnerable, but an abandonment denial cannot be appealed (8 CFR 103.2(b)(15)). Options: (a) a motion to reopen with USCIS (Form I-290B) under 8 CFR 103.5(a), showing the RFE was sent to the wrong address; the regular 30-day (33 mailed) deadline passed (December 2023), but USCIS may excuse delay where it was reasonable and beyond the filer's control, and it can reopen on its own motion; (b) a new I-130 filed by the wife (a denial for abandonment does not preclude refiling), which is the more reliable route. Because a new I-130 is stronger if filed with a request to be adjudicated in connection with the IJ proceedings, file it promptly. Fee for I-130 is a USCIS fee (check current USCIS schedule; not verified here).

4. THE I-485 DENIAL. An I-485 denial is not appealable to the AAO (8 CFR 103.3 and 245.2(a)(5)(ii)), but the applicant may renew the application in removal proceedings before the IJ. Once the case is reopened, the husband can request adjustment before the IJ as an immediate relative of a U.S. citizen: INA 245(a) allows adjustment for those inspected and admitted; INA 245(c)(2) bars most overstays but exempts immediate relatives (INA 245(c)). The I-485 denial itself was, by regulation, a consequence of the I-130 denial; if a valid I-130 is approved, the IJ can adjudicate adjustment. Because the IJ cannot adjudicate an I-130, USCIS must approve it (or the case can be continued).

5. MAJOR RISK. He entered on a B-2 visa on December 1, 2022, married 19 days later and filed 31 days after entry. Under the State Department 90-day rule (9 FAM 302.9-4) and USCIS practice, conduct inconsistent with the visa status within 90 days raises a presumption of willful misrepresentation under INA 212(a)(6)(C)(i), which would make him inadmissible (waivable with I-601 only with a qualifying USC spouse and extreme hardship). The couple should be prepared to rebut this with evidence of bona fide marriage and absence of preconceived intent. (This is from general knowledge, not verified in this run.)

6. Also consider: asking ICE OPLA to join a motion to reopen (joint motion/prosecutorial discretion), and a motion to reopen based on sua sponte authority (8 CFR 1003.23(b)(1)) as a back-up. Seek counsel; the 2026 EOIR environment is enforcement-heavy.
